svg.aria-label: Diagram: A CloudWatch Logs subscription filter provides a real-time feed of log events to AWS Lambda, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams or Amazon Data Firehose, delivered soon after ingestion and usually in less than three minutes, with events compressed in gzip format and Lambda receiving them base64 encoded in the awslogs.data field. Each account can have one account-level subscription filter per Region and each log group can have up to five subscription filters, and subscriptions are supported only for log groups in the Standard log class. The delivery contract has two halves that behave in opposite directions. If the destination returns a retryable error such as a throttling exception or a retryable service exception like an HTTP 5xx, CloudWatch Logs continues to retry delivery for up to 24 hours, so events arrive late. If the error is non-retryable, such as AccessDeniedException or ResourceNotFoundException, CloudWatch Logs does not try to re-deliver: the subscription filter is disabled for up to 10 minutes and then retried, and during that disabled period logs are skipped, so the two most common misconfigurations produce silent loss in a repeating cycle while the log group itself still holds every event. On the good path the guarantee is at-least-once delivery with duplicate events possible, and batching may be used to optimise transmission but is not guaranteed, so a consumer must be idempotent and must handle both single events and batches. With log transformation in place the filter pattern is compared to the transformed versions of the log events. Visibility comes from per-minute metrics in the AWS slash Logs namespace: DeliveryErrors counts log events for which an error was received when forwarding, DeliveryThrottling counts events for which forwarding was throttled, and ForwardedLogEvents and ForwardedBytes count what did arrive, all carrying LogGroupName, DestinationType, FilterName and PolicyLevel dimensions so an alarm can name the broken filter, with the ratio of ForwardedLogEvents to IncomingLogEvents over time as a second signal. Finally there is a recursion hazard: a subscription filter on a log group that receives events as a result of the subscription delivery workflow creates an infinite loop with a large increase in ingestion billing, the documented example being Firehose to S3 to a Lambda whose own log group is subscribed, and a VPC flow log group can cause the same loop. The remedy is excluding those log groups with the selectionCriteria parameter of PutAccountPolicy, though log events produced by a Lambda destination's own log group are already not forwarded back for an account-level policy.
svg.title: Retryable errors wait; non-retryable errors skip the logs
svg.text: The patient path handles their failure. The lossy path handles yours.
“Log events are sent to the receiving resource soon after being ingested, usually less than three minutes.”
RETRYABLE — THROTTLING, HTTP 5xx
“continues to retry delivery for up to 24 hours”
The events wait. They arrive late.
Cause: the destination is busy.
Fix it within a day and you lose nothing at all.
NON-RETRYABLE — ACCESSDENIED, NOTFOUND
“disabled for up to 10 minutes … logs are skipped”
Then it retries. Fails. Disables again.
Cause: you changed something.
An hour unnoticed is an hour of holes, permanently.
And the log group is perfect throughout
Every event still in CloudWatch Logs, queryable, complete. Only the copy that went to your SIEM is missing.
Two systems disagree, neither is broken, and the wrong one is the one your detections run on.
THE CONSUMER’S SHARE
“at least one time delivery … duplicate events may
occasionally occur” — so be idempotent.
“Batching is not guaranteed but is used when possible.”
One event or many — the same code path must take both.
WHAT MAKES IT VISIBLE
DeliveryErrors alarm on this, per FilterName
DeliveryThrottling the patient path, working
Forwarded vs Incoming ratio over time
Published every minute. Dimensioned by filter name.
The recursion loop, which is a billing event
“… a subscription filter is associated with a log group that receives log events as a result of your
subscription delivery workflow.” Firehose → S3 → Lambda → its own subscribed log group → round again.
The one people miss: the VPC flow log group of the network the destination function runs in.
Capacity: five subscription filters per log group, one account-level filter per Region, Standard log class only.
Each filter fails independently — one being disabled says nothing about the other four.
An export is a job you can re-run. A subscription is a stream, and a skipped window does not come back.
Alarm on the delivery, not on the log group. When you must prove it happened, go back to the log group.
